title: Space & Territory
hook: People defend a chair, a desk or a side of the bed as if it were their skin, and the markers they leave tell you what they think they own.
why:
The chapter on proxemics described the bubble of space people carry around with them. This chapter is about something different: the places people claim and defend even when they are not standing in them. A regular seat at the pub. A desk in a shared office. A side of the bed. A chair at the family table that nobody else sits in. A parking space outside the house that is, legally, anyone's.

People feel these claims strongly, and they react to violations of them with an intensity that often surprises everyone involved, themselves included. The research on territory explains why, and it gives a reader a rich source of information. You will learn the kinds of territory and how they differ, how people mark their claims and how others respect the markers, what happens when territory is invaded, why people behave differently on their own ground, what rooms reveal about the people who use them, why losing territory can hurt far more than it seems it should, and how to read and respect the claims around you, including your own.

teach.h: Territory is space with a claim on it.
teach.p:
Personal space travels with you. Territory stays put. The social psychologist Irwin Altman, writing in 1975, distinguished three kinds of territory according to how strong and lasting the claim is.

Primary territories are owned and used exclusively and over long periods, and are central to a person's sense of who they are: a home, a bedroom, sometimes a car or a private office. Intrusion into them is felt as a serious violation. Secondary territories are used regularly and claimed informally, but not owned: a regular seat at the pub, a desk in a shared office, a particular table at the café, a bench in the park where the same group of friends always meets. The claim is real but negotiable, and disputes over secondary territories are common. Public territories are claimed only temporarily and only while in use: a table in a library, a spot on a beach, a seat on a train.

The kinds shade into one another. A family dinner table is a primary territory for the family, and each person's chair at it may be a small primary territory within it. A teenager's bedroom is often the first primary territory a young person can call their own, which is why its door matters so much.

For a reader, the useful question about any space is: whose is it, and how strongly? A man sitting in someone else's regular seat, a new colleague at a desk that used to be another's, a guest who settles into the host's armchair: each has stepped into a claim, and the people around will often react before anyone says a word.

Ask whose space it is before you read how people behave in it.
teach.disconfirm: If people reacted to the use of their regular seat, desk or chair no more strongly than to the use of any other seat, the idea of secondary territory would add nothing. Watch what happens the next time someone sits in a seat that is usually someone else's.

teach.p:
People leave objects behind to hold their claims: a coat on a chair, a towel on a sunbed, a bag on a library table, a mug on a desk, a jacket over the back of a seat in a meeting room. In the late 1960s and early 1970s Robert Sommer and Franklin Becker studied these markers in libraries and canteens.

Markers worked. Tables with personal belongings left on them were avoided by newcomers for much longer than empty tables, and the more personal the marker, a jacket rather than a stack of library magazines, the longer it held the space. Neighbours took part in the defence too. When a newcomer approached a marked seat, people sitting nearby would often tell them it was taken, defending a claim that was not theirs.

Markers are a language almost everyone understands without being taught. They also tell you something about how people see their place. The colleague who covers a hot desk with photographs, a plant and a personal mug every morning is claiming more than a work surface. The guest who leaves their bag by the door rather than unpacking is keeping a light claim. The partner who keeps a toothbrush at your flat but no clothes has marked a particular level of belonging.

Changes in marking are worth noticing. A person who stops personalising their desk, clears away their photographs or leaves their coat on rather than hanging it up may be loosening their claim on the place: thinking of leaving, feeling unwelcome, or simply busy. As always, the change is a reason to look more closely, not a conclusion.

Read the objects people leave behind. They are claims written in things.
teach.disconfirm: If personal markers left on tables or seats in public places turned out to keep newcomers away no longer than no markers at all, the marker findings would not hold where you live. Watching a busy café for an hour will usually settle it.

teach.h: Invasion brings flight, and sometimes a fight.
teach.p:
In 1966 Nancy Felipe and Robert Sommer ran a simple and slightly uncomfortable experiment. A researcher sat down right next to people who were sitting alone, on benches in the grounds of a hospital and at large, mostly empty tables in a university library, close enough to invade their space but saying nothing. People who were invaded in this way left much sooner than similar people who were left alone. Many first tried to restore their space by shifting, turning away or building a barrier of books and bags.

Responses to territorial invasion can also be oddly hostile. In 1997 Barry Ruback and Daniel Juieng watched drivers leaving spaces in a shopping-centre car park. Drivers took longer to leave when another car was waiting for their space, and longer still when the waiting driver sounded the horn, even though staying longer served no purpose. People defended a space they were about to give up anyway, against someone who had a perfectly good reason to want it, and few of them would have described what they were doing as defence.

These responses are worth recognising in others and in yourself. The irritation you feel when someone takes your usual seat, the urge to linger in a parking space someone is waiting for, the sharp words over a shared fridge shelf, are territorial responses, and they are usually out of proportion to the material stakes. Knowing that does not make them disappear, but it can stop you from reading them as something more personal than they are.

When a dispute over space seems far more heated than the space deserves, territory is often the reason.
teach.disconfirm: If drivers left parking spaces just as quickly when someone was waiting, or faster, territorial lingering would not be operating in your setting. Try timing a few departures with and without a waiting car, from a discreet distance.
teach.pullQuote: When a dispute over space seems more heated than the space deserves, territory is often the reason.

teach.p:
Sports teams win more often at home, a finding so consistent across sports and decades that researchers treat it as one of the most reliable patterns in the field, though its causes are debated. Something similar happens in ordinary life. In 2011 Graham Brown and Markus Baer set up negotiations in which one party was on their own territory, an office they had been given time to make their own, and the other was a visitor. Negotiators on home ground tended to achieve better outcomes, and the researchers linked the advantage to the greater confidence people felt in their own space.

For a reader, this means that behaviour has to be read against whose territory it is. A man who is quiet and careful in your office may be expansive and funny in his workshop, his kitchen or his club. A child who is shy at school may be bossy at home. A colleague who seems hesitant in head office may be decisive on the shop floor she runs. Each of them is showing a real part of themselves, and neither setting gives you the whole picture.

It also suggests a courtesy. If you want to understand someone, or want them to feel at ease, meet them on their ground or on neutral ground, rather than summoning them to yours. A manager who visits a team member's workspace to talk, rather than calling them to his office, is giving up a little home advantage, and often gets a franker conversation in return.

And when you are the visitor, remember that part of what you feel, the slight awkwardness, the deference to your host's habits, is the territory speaking, not the person.

Before you judge how someone behaves, notice whose ground you are both standing on.
teach.disconfirm: If people you know behaved in just the same way on their own ground, on yours and on neutral ground, territory would not be shaping their behaviour much. Compare one person you know well in two or three settings before deciding.

teach.p:
In 2002 Sam Gosling and colleagues sent observers into the offices and bedrooms of people they had never met, and asked them to rate the occupants' personalities from the rooms alone. The observers agreed with each other strongly, and on some traits they were reasonably accurate when compared with the occupants' own ratings and those of people who knew them. Openness to new experience was the easiest to judge, from the range of books, music and objects. Conscientiousness showed in how organised the space was.

Gosling described two kinds of clue. Identity claims are deliberate statements: posters, photographs, awards, flags, the objects a person chooses to display to say who they are or wish to be. Behavioural residue is what everyday life leaves behind without any intention: the piled papers, the empty mugs, the worn path in a carpet. Both are informative, and they can disagree, which is itself interesting.

Rooms are a powerful source of information, and that is exactly why they need the ethics described in Part VI. A room you are invited into is information shared under the norms of the invitation. A colleague's open office during a meeting is one thing; their drawers are another. Reading a friend's bookshelves while they make tea is ordinary curiosity. Reading their post is not. The chapter on the ethics of reading people calls this contextual integrity: the question is not only what you can see, but where the information was offered and where it may go.

Rooms also mislead. A sparse office may belong to someone who has just moved in, or works mostly elsewhere, or shares the room, or simply keeps their life at home. A cluttered one may belong to someone far more organised than it looks.

Read a room as a person's claims, and remember that claims are not the whole person.
teach.disconfirm: If observers' judgments of people from their rooms turned out to agree neither with each other nor with the occupants, rooms would tell you nothing. The study found strong agreement and some accuracy, which is enough to be useful and not enough to be sure.

teach.p:
Because territory is bound up with identity, losing it can feel like a loss of self. In 2003 Kimberly Elsbach studied employees whose company moved from assigned desks to a system in which nobody had a fixed place. Many described the change as a threat to their sense of who they were at work. Without a desk to personalise, they lost a way of showing their status, their distinctiveness and their place in the team, and some found ways to reclaim it: arriving early to get the same desk every day, carrying their belongings around in boxes, or claiming particular corners as their own.

The same pattern appears far beyond offices. A man who retires loses not only a job but a desk, a parking space, a workshop, a seat in meetings. A family that moves house loses rooms full of history. A parent whose children leave home finds their territory changed. A widower faces the empty side of the bed. A teenager who must share a bedroom with a new step-sibling loses the first space that was theirs alone.

Territorial loss often shows itself indirectly. People become irritable about small encroachments, over-mark the space they still have, guard objects more closely, or withdraw from shared spaces altogether. These behaviours are easy to misread as bad temper or rudeness. Read against a recent loss of territory, they often make immediate sense.

When someone's behaviour around space changes, ask what space they have lost.

And when you are the cause of someone's territorial loss, as a new partner moving in, a manager reorganising an office, a new step-parent, give them some space that is clearly and lastingly theirs. It costs little and it settles a great deal.
teach.disconfirm: If people who had recently lost an important territory, such as a desk, a room or a home, behaved no differently around space than people who had not, the link between territory and identity would be weak. In your own experience, think of one such change and what followed.

teach.h: Read the claims, and respect them.
teach.p:
Bring this together into a few practical habits. When you enter a space, notice its claims: whose desk, whose seat, whose side, whose marker. When behaviour in a space seems puzzling, ask whose territory it is and whether anyone has recently gained or lost some. When a dispute about space is out of proportion to the stakes, consider that it may be about belonging rather than the space itself.

Respect claims, including small ones. Ask before using someone's desk or chair, even when it is technically shared. Knock on a teenager's door and wait. Do not move someone's marker without asking. When someone new joins a household or a team, give them a place that is clearly theirs, a drawer, a shelf, a desk, a peg for their coat, and you will often see them settle faster.

Notice your own claims too. Most people underestimate how much space they take in shared places: the bag on the seat beside them on a busy train, the papers spread across a shared table, the wide stance on a crowded bench, the car that always takes the best space. Others read these claims as clearly as you read theirs, and they form impressions of you from them.

Finally, remember that some people have very little territory of their own: the person sharing a room in a hostel, the patient on a ward, the carer who lives in someone else's house. Small gestures of respect for the scraps of space they do have, knocking, asking, not touching their things, can matter to them a great deal.

Territory is identity with walls. Treat it accordingly.
teach.disconfirm: If respecting people's small territorial claims, by asking and knocking, made no difference to how comfortable they were with you, the advice in this block would add nothing. Try it with one person for a month and ask them afterwards.

poseGallery.doCaption: Taking only your share of it.
poseGallery.annotation: Others read your territorial claims as clearly as you read theirs. Taking more than your share of a shared space is noticed.

poseGallery.doCaption: Knocking, and waiting at the door.
poseGallery.dontCaption: Walking straight into a teenager's room.
poseGallery.annotation: A bedroom is often a young person's first primary territory. Respecting its door respects the person.

poseGallery.doCaption: Choosing a place at a respectful distance.
poseGallery.dontCaption: Sitting right beside the one person on an empty bench.
poseGallery.annotation: Felipe and Sommer found that people invaded in this way left much sooner. Unnecessary closeness in public space is felt as invasion.

poseGallery.dontCaption: Treating a colleague's desk as yours to use.
poseGallery.annotation: Secondary territories are claimed informally but felt strongly. A quick question avoids a surprising amount of resentment.

poseGallery.doCaption: Perched, waiting to be shown a seat
poseGallery.dontCaption: Sprawling in the host's own chair
poseGallery.annotation: In someone else's home, wait to be offered a seat. Many chairs belong to someone, even if nobody says so.

poseGallery.doCaption: Meeting on neutral ground, side by side
poseGallery.dontCaption: Calling the hard talk into your own office
poseGallery.annotation: Home ground gives the host an edge. When fairness matters, choose a place that belongs to neither of you.

caseStudy:
Frank, sixty-three, retires after forty years as an engineer. For the first few weeks he enjoys being at home. Then he starts helping in the kitchen. He reorganises the cupboards so that things are where he thinks they should be, rearranges the drawer of utensils, and takes over the Sunday cooking. His wife, Linda, who has run the kitchen for thirty-five years, becomes short with him. They argue about where the colander should live. Frank tells a friend that retirement is putting a strain on the marriage.

His friend asks a question Frank has not considered: what did he lose when he retired? Frank thinks about it. He lost a desk he had sat at for fifteen years, a parking space with his name on it, a workshop where everyone knew which tools were his, and a seat at the end of the Monday meeting. And he has been trying, without realising it, to claim new territory in the one room that was most clearly Linda's.

That evening he asks Linda, carefully, whether he has been taking over the kitchen. She laughs, a little sharply, and says yes, and that she has started to feel like a guest in her own house. They put the cupboards back the way she had them.

Frank clears out the garden shed, which has been full of junk for years, and turns it into a workshop with a bench, a radio and a pegboard for his tools. He joins a volunteer group that repairs bicycles for a local charity, and within a month he has a regular place at the end of their bench too. He still cooks on Sundays, when Linda asks him to, and he asks where things are.

The arguments stop. Linda tells her sister that Frank seems more himself. Frank thinks it is because he has somewhere to be himself in.
observe: In a café, library or train, notice the markers people leave to hold their places, and how newcomers respond to them.
Notice the seats in your home or workplace that are usually taken by the same person, and what happens when someone else sits in one.
Notice your own territorial claims in a shared space today, such as a bag on a seat or papers on a table, and how much space they take.

drills.name: Territory Map
steps: Draw a simple plan of your home or workplace.
Mark each space as primary, secondary or public territory, and for whom.
Note any space whose ownership is unclear or disputed.
Mark any space that has recently changed hands or been lost by someone.
Write one sentence about any tension you have noticed around those spaces.
variations: Do the same for a place you visit often but do not own, such as your parents' home or a friend's, and mark whose territory each part is.
Ask someone else who uses the same space to draw their own map, and compare the two.
Mark the places where you feel most and least at ease, and see whether they match the kinds of territory.

drills.name: Marker Watch
steps: In a busy café, library or waiting room, watch for personal markers left on tables and seats.
For each, note what the marker was and how long it held the space.
Note how newcomers responded to marked and unmarked places.
Note any time a neighbour defended a marked place.
Write down which kinds of marker seemed strongest.
variations: Count how long marked and unmarked tables stay empty in the same room, and compare personal markers with impersonal ones.
Watch a beach, pool or park on a busy day and note the range of markers people use.

drills.name: Whose Ground
steps: Choose one person you know well and recall how they behave in two different settings, such as their home and your workplace.
Note differences in their volume, posture, humour and decisiveness.
Consider whose territory each setting was.
Write down which version of them you had been treating as the real one.
Plan one conversation with them on their ground or neutral ground, and note any difference.
variations: Choose someone you manage or teach, and think about which version of them you see on your ground.
Ask the person which setting they find easiest for difficult conversations, and use it next time.

drills.name: Room Reading, Ethically
steps: The next time you are invited into someone's home or office, notice what is on display without touching or opening anything.
Separate what you see into identity claims, such as photographs and posters, and behavioural residue, such as clutter and wear.
Afterwards, write two impressions the room gave you.
For each impression, write one ordinary explanation that would make it misleading.
Do not share your impressions with anyone else.
variations: Do the same with your own room or home, imagining a stranger seeing it for the first time.
Notice your own video call background and write what it might suggest to someone who does not know you.

drills.name: Your Claims
steps: For one day, notice every territorial claim you make in shared spaces, such as seats, tables, desks, fridges and parking.
Note how much space each takes, compared with what you need.
Notice whether anyone had to work around one of your claims.
Choose one claim to reduce.
Note whether anyone seems to notice the difference.
variations: Choose a shared space such as a train, office kitchen or gym, and note how much of it your belongings occupy.
At home, ask someone you live with which of your territorial habits they would most like you to change.

quiz.q: Drivers leaving a car-park space are watched by another driver waiting for it. What did Ruback and Juieng find?
options: Drivers left noticeably faster, out of courtesy to the person waiting
Drivers left at exactly the same speed whether anyone was waiting or not
Drivers took longer when someone was waiting, as if defending the space
Drivers left the space only after making eye contact with the waiting driver
quiz.explain: Drivers lingered when someone was waiting, and longer still if honked at. Territorial responses are often out of proportion to the stakes, and people rarely notice them in themselves.

quiz.q: In Irwin Altman's terms, what kind of territory is your regular seat at a local pub?
options: Secondary: used regularly and claimed, but not owned
Primary: owned, exclusive and central to your identity
Public: temporary, and held only while you sit in it
Not territory at all, since nobody owns a seat in a pub
quiz.explain: Secondary territories are claimed informally through regular use. The claim is real and felt strongly, but it is negotiable, which is why disputes over them are so common.

quiz.q: What did Gosling and colleagues find when strangers judged people's personalities from their offices and bedrooms?
options: They could judge nothing at all beyond how tidy each room was
They were wrong about every trait they were asked to judge
They judged accurately only when shown photos of the occupant
They agreed strongly, and judged some traits fairly accurately
quiz.explain: Observers agreed with each other and were reasonably accurate on some traits, especially openness. Rooms carry real information, which is why reading them needs the ethics of where that information was offered.

quiz.q: Your teenage son has started keeping his bedroom door closed and objects when you walk in without knocking. What fits this chapter?
options: Insist on an open door, since a closed one means he is hiding something
Treat it as an ordinary claim on his territory; knock and wait
Take the door off its hinges until he explains what is going on
Search the room while he is out to make sure nothing is wrong
quiz.explain: A bedroom is often a young person's first primary territory, and claiming it is ordinary. Respecting the door respects him; real concerns about safety are a reason to talk with him, not to invade the space.

quiz.q: In Felipe and Sommer's study, what happened when a researcher sat right beside people sitting alone on benches and at library tables?
options: They moved closer to the researcher and began conversations
They took no notice and stayed for the same length of time
They left much sooner than people who were not approached
They asked the researcher to move, politely, in almost every case
quiz.explain: Invaded people first tried to restore their space by shifting, turning or building barriers, and then left. Unnecessary closeness in a public place is felt as invasion even without a word.

quiz.q: After your office moves to hot-desking, a usually easy-going colleague turns irritable and arrives early every day to claim the same desk. What fits?
options: Losing his own desk may feel like a threat to his identity; he is reclaiming one
He is being selfish and should be told to use a different desk each day
He is unhappy with the company and is probably planning to leave soon
He is anxious about something at home and needs the routine to cope
quiz.explain: Studies of desk-sharing found many people experienced losing a fixed place as a threat to who they were at work, and reclaimed space in just this way. Read against a territorial loss, his behaviour makes sense.

quiz.q: In Altman's terms, what kind of territory is a person's own bedroom?
options: Public territory, since anyone may enter it when it is not being used by its owner at the time
Primary territory, owned and used exclusively over long periods and tied to identity
Secondary territory, claimed informally through regular use but not owned by anyone at all
No territory at all, since territory applies only to spaces outside the home and work
quiz.explain: Primary territories are owned and used exclusively, and are central to a person's sense of who they are. Intrusion into them is felt as a serious violation, which is why knocking on a teenager's door matters so much.

quiz.q: What did Sommer and Becker find about markers left to hold places in libraries and canteens?
options: Markers had no effect, since newcomers sat wherever they liked regardless of objects left
Only markers left by staff were respected, while those left by other users were ignored
Markers held places, and more personal markers, such as a jacket, held them for longer
Markers worked only while the owner was in sight, and were ignored as soon as they left
quiz.explain: Marked places were avoided by newcomers for longer than empty ones, and personal markers worked best. Objects speak for absent owners, which is why moving someone's things can feel like a small invasion.

quiz.q: A colleague says that people negotiate equally well wherever a meeting is held. What did Brown and Baer's research suggest?
options: She is right, since skill in negotiation is not affected by where the meeting takes place
She is right only for experienced negotiators, who are not affected by their surroundings
She is wrong, but only because visitors tend to make more generous offers out of politeness
Negotiators on their own ground tended to do better, and visitors felt less confident
quiz.explain: Home ground gave negotiators an advantage in Brown and Baer's studies, partly through confidence and partly through the rituals of hosting. That is a reason to choose neutral ground when fairness matters.

quiz.q: At the first family dinner since your father died, his usual chair at the head of the table is empty. What fits this chapter best?
options: Ask your mother beforehand what she would like done with the chair this year
Sit in it yourself, so that nobody has to look at an empty chair through the meal
Remove it from the room before anyone arrives, to spare everyone the sadness
Leave it, say nothing, and let whoever arrives first decide what to do with it
quiz.explain: A place like that is primary territory that has outlived its owner, and it often becomes a kind of memorial. The decision belongs, first, to the person closest to it, and asking her lets the family choose together.

reflection.prompt: Think of one specific territory that matters to you, a seat, a desk, a room, a side of the bed, a place at a table. How would you feel if someone else began using it without asking? Then think of a time when you gained or lost a territory, by moving house, changing jobs, retiring or someone new joining your household. How did your behaviour around space change afterwards? What did the people around you make of it?
reflection.guidance: Most people are surprised by how strongly they feel about a space they do not even own. The second part is often where the insight lies: behaviour that looked like bad temper to others may have been a response to a territorial loss that nobody named. Naming it, to yourself and to the people affected, is often enough to ease it.

failureMode: The commonest failure is to miss territory altogether and read territorial behaviour as personality: the colleague who guards his desk as possessive, the parent who snaps about the kitchen as irritable, the teenager who closes his door as secretive. The second is to ignore other people's claims, sitting in the regular seat, using the shared desk without asking, moving someone's things, and then being surprised by the reaction. The third is to read rooms without ethics, treating anything visible as yours to examine and discuss. And the fourth is to forget your own claims, taking more than your share of shared space while resenting others who do the same. Ask whose space it is, respect small claims, and remember that territory is identity with walls.

moreCases.title: Grandad's chair
moreCases.scene:
Every Christmas for thirty years, the Hughes family has eaten at the same long table, and every year Grandad Ken sat at the head of it,
  in a high-backed wooden chair nobody else used. Ken died in the spring. At Christmas, the family gathers for the first time without him.
  Ken's son, Mark, arrives a little late, sees that the head of the table is empty, and, thinking to save everyone the awkwardness of looking
  at an empty chair, sits in it.

  His mother, Jean, goes very quiet. She serves the meal without looking at him and leaves the room twice. Mark's sister, Claire, kicks him
  under the table. After dinner, in the kitchen, Jean tells Mark sharply that he could have asked. Mark is wounded. He had meant it kindly, he
  says, and it is only a chair. Jean says nothing more, but she is cool with him for the rest of the holiday.

Claire, who stayed later than the others, found her mother in the kitchen at midnight, holding one of Ken's pipes that she had kept on the shelf by his chair. Jean said that she had been dreading the day for weeks, and that the chair was the part she had not known how to face.
moreCases.misread:
Mark read the empty chair as a practical problem: a gap at the table that would make everyone sad. He did not read it as territory, a place bound up with his father's identity and his mother's marriage, or consider that sitting in it might feel to his mother like taking something that was not his to take.

He also read his mother's coolness as an overreaction to a small thing, which made it harder for him to see the large thing underneath it.
moreCases.betterRead:
Altman's primary territories are places tied closely to a person's sense of who they are, and they can outlive the person. A chair at the head of a family table is exactly that kind of place, and after a death it often becomes a kind of memorial. The careful reading notices the claim before acting on it: whose place is this, and who else might feel it is theirs to decide? Mark could have asked his mother, before the meal, what she wanted done with the chair this year. Some families leave it empty; some ask the eldest to take it; some put a photograph on it. Any of these would have been fine. What made it hurt was that the decision was taken without her.

It is worth adding that grief makes territory more sensitive, not less. In the first year after a death, many families find that rooms, chairs and objects matter more than they would have predicted, and a question costs far less than an assumption.

moreCases.title: The fridge shelf
moreCases.scene:
Four people share a flat in a city where none of them grew up. Each has a shelf in the fridge, agreed on the day they moved in. Over a
  few weeks, Josh, the newest flatmate, starts putting his overflow on the shelf belonging to Eilidh, who is away most weekends. One Sunday
  evening Eilidh comes home to find her shelf full of Josh's beer and a half-eaten lasagne, and her own milk pushed to the back.

  She takes everything of his off her shelf and puts it on the counter. Josh comes home, finds his lasagne warm on the side, and is furious.
  The row that follows is far louder than anyone expects, and goes on for an hour, taking in washing up, noise, guests and who pays for toilet
  roll. The other two flatmates retreat to their rooms. For the next month, Josh and Eilidh barely speak.

The two flatmates who retreated to their rooms later admitted that they too had been using other people's shelves now and then, and that the row had frightened them because it showed how much was riding on such small things.

Afterwards each of them tells friends a version of the story in which the other is the problem. In Josh's version Eilidh threw his food on the floor; in Eilidh's version Josh had taken over her half of the fridge for weeks. Neither version mentions that Eilidh is away so often, or why she minds so much.
moreCases.misread:
Each read the other's behaviour as a personal attack and a sign of character: Josh was selfish and careless, Eilidh petty and uptight. Neither recognised that the argument was not really about a shelf. It was about whether each of them had a secure place in a home where they were all, in a sense, guests.

The flatmates who stayed out of the row read it the same way, and quietly took sides according to whom they liked more, which made the flat a little colder for everyone.

It is also worth noticing that neither of them could have said, in the moment, what the shelf meant to them. The anger came first and the explanation much later.
moreCases.betterRead:
In shared homes, small secondary territories carry far more weight than they seem to, because they are the only parts of the home that are clearly one person's. A shelf, a cupboard, a hook for a coat: each is a claim to belong. A dispute that is out of proportion to its stakes, as this chapter's last teaching point says, is often about belonging rather than the space itself. The careful move, for either of them, was to name that. Josh might have asked before borrowing the shelf, and Eilidh might have said that her shelf mattered to her because she was away so much and needed one thing in the flat that was reliably hers. Most flat rows end faster once someone says what the space means.

Josh and Eilidh did eventually talk, at the prompting of one of the others. Josh admitted he had not thought of the shelf as anything more than space. Eilidh admitted that she had been feeling like a lodger in her own flat. They have been friendly since.

moreCases.title: Negotiating on their ground
moreCases.scene:
Rachel runs a small marketing firm and is negotiating the renewal of a contract with a large client. The client's procurement manager,
  Simon, insists that the meeting take place at the client's headquarters. Rachel and her colleague are shown into a meeting room on the
  fourth floor, given visitor badges, and kept waiting fifteen minutes. Simon arrives with two colleagues, sits at the head of the table on the side
  facing the window, and leaves the visitors facing the light.

  Rachel feels off balance from the start. She concedes more than she intended on price, agrees to a longer notice period, and drives home
  frustrated with herself. Her colleague says that Simon seemed very sure of himself, and that perhaps they had simply been out-negotiated.

On the drive home, Rachel's colleague mentions that he could barely see Simon's face for the glare from the window behind him, and that he had spent most of the meeting squinting. Rachel realises she had done the same.

At the next meeting, three months later, Simon again suggests his office. This time Rachel notices the arrangement as it happens: the wait in reception, the seat against the window, the colleague who arrives with a pre-printed agenda. She does not feel any more confident, but she knows why she feels unsettled, which turns out to help.
moreCases.misread:
Rachel read the outcome as a matter of personal skill: Simon was the better negotiator, and she had been weak. She did not notice how much of the meeting had been arranged by territory: his building, his room, his choice of seat, the wait, the badges, the light in her eyes.

She also missed the small signals that the room had been arranged deliberately. Leaving visitors to wait and face the light is not always an accident.

Her colleague's conclusion, that they had simply been out-negotiated, was the most discouraging explanation available, and the least useful, because it suggested nothing they could do differently.
moreCases.betterRead:
Brown and Baer found that negotiators on their own ground tend to achieve better outcomes, and that visitors tend to feel less confident. Some of that comes from familiarity and some from the small rituals of hosting, which put the host in charge of time, seating and comfort. A reader who understands this can reduce its effect without any tricks: by suggesting a neutral venue, or alternating venues across a series of meetings, or simply by noticing the effect and allowing for it, taking a moment to settle, asking to swap seats if the light is in your eyes, and saying that you will need to consider the terms before agreeing. For the next renewal, Rachel proposed meeting at a hotel halfway between the two offices. Simon agreed, and the negotiation was noticeably more even.

When you lose a negotiation away from home, part of the loss may belong to the room. Knowing that stops you drawing the wrong conclusion about your own ability, and asking for small things at the start, a seat, some water, restores more footing than you expect.

moreCases.title: The parking space outside number twelve
moreCases.scene:
In a terraced street where nobody has a driveway, Dennis, seventy-four, has parked outside his own house for twenty-six years. The space is
  public road; anyone can use it. When a new family moves in three doors down and starts parking there, Dennis first leaves a polite note on their
  windscreen, then a less polite one, then starts putting a wheelie bin in the space whenever he drives out. The new neighbour, Tariq, moves the bin
  and parks anyway. Within a month, the two men are not speaking, and Dennis has complained to the council.

  Tariq thinks Dennis is a bully who believes he owns the street. Dennis thinks Tariq is arrogant and disrespectful. Both feel entirely in the
  right. Neither has ever spoken to the other face to face.

Tariq's wife, who has noticed Dennis watching from his window each morning, wonders aloud whether he is lonely. Tariq says that is not their problem.

Dennis's daughter, who visits on Sundays, tells him he is making himself ill over a parking space. He tells her that she does not understand; that the space is the only one near enough to the front door for him to carry the shopping, and that the street used to be full of people who knew that without being told.
moreCases.misread:
Tariq read Dennis's markers and complaints as entitlement and hostility, and Dennis read Tariq's parking as a deliberate provocation. Each responded to the other's moves with a stronger move of his own, which is exactly the escalation that territorial disputes produce when the claims are never discussed.

The council complaint made things worse, because it moved the dispute from two neighbours into an institution, where neither could back down without losing face.

Each also read the other's silence as hostility, when it was mostly the ordinary reluctance of two strangers to knock on a door.
moreCases.betterRead:
Ruback and Juieng's study of drivers leaving car park spaces found that people took longer to leave when someone was waiting for the space, and longer still when the waiting driver sounded the horn: people defend even spaces they are about to abandon. A space outside your own house for twenty-six years is a far stronger claim, legally empty but emotionally full. The careful reading starts from that. For Dennis, the space may be tied to his age, his mobility and his sense that the street is changing around him. A neighbour who knocks on the door, introduces himself and asks how the parking usually works on this street will often find an old man who wants to be acknowledged more than he wants the space. Tariq did that, eventually, at his wife's urging. Dennis told him about his bad hip. They agreed that Tariq would leave the space free in the evenings.

It is worth noticing that the solution was not about the space at all. The evenings were when Dennis came home with shopping; the mornings mattered to nobody. Nobody could have found that out through notes and bins.

workedReading.title: Moving into her flat
workedReading.scene:
Tom moves into his girlfriend Leah's flat after a year together. It has been her home for five years. The first fortnight goes well. In the third week, Tom notices that Leah has become short with him in the evenings. She sighs when he comes in, tidies around him, and twice moves his things from the living room back into the spare room without saying anything. One evening, when he sits in the armchair by the window with his laptop, she says, "Can you not sit there?" and then apologises and says it does not matter.

Tom loves Leah and was excited to move in. He has been trying to make himself at home, which he thought was what she wanted.

steps.label: Check yourself
steps.text:
Tom's first reaction is hurt, followed by a worry that the move was a mistake and that she has changed her mind about living with him. He notices that worry and decides to treat it as a feeling, not a finding. He also notices that he has been tired and stressed at work, and has spent more evenings than usual on his laptop.

He also notices that he has been reading her sighs as verdicts on him rather than as information about how her days are going, which they might equally be.

steps.label: Map the territory
steps.text:
Tom thinks about the flat in Altman's terms. For Leah it is primary territory, built up over five years and tied to her sense of herself. For him it is, so far, somewhere between secondary and borrowed. Within it, some places are especially hers: the armchair by the window where she reads, the bedside table, the shelf of books in the living room. He realises he has used all of them without thinking.

It helps to think about what he would feel if the roles were reversed: if Leah had moved into a flat he had lived in for five years, and was now reading in his chair every evening.

steps.label: Notice the markers
steps.text:
He looks at what has changed in the flat since he arrived. His laptop and charger now live on the coffee table. His coat hangs on the hook she used. His shoes are by the door where hers used to be. His books are stacked on the floor beside her shelf. None of these was a decision; they just happened. Together, they spread his claims across most of the living space.

Markers matter even when the owner is not trying to claim anything. To Leah, the flat now speaks with Tom's voice in every room, and hers has gone quiet.

Seeing the flat through her eyes for a moment, he realises that it now looks more like his than hers, and that he did all of this in three weeks, without once asking.

steps.label: Note the timing
steps.text:
The shortness started in the third week, not the first, and it is worst in the evenings, when both of them are home and using the same rooms. The comment about the chair came when he sat in the one place she goes to unwind. The pattern points to the space and the hours, not to the relationship as a whole.

Timing also tells him that something accumulated. A week of small claims did not register; three weeks of them did.

steps.label: Hold several explanations
steps.text:
Several stories fit. Leah is having second thoughts. She is stressed about something else, at work or with family. She is finding it harder than she expected to share the flat that has been hers. Or all of the territorial changes together have left her without a corner of her own. The timing and the chair favour the last two, without ruling out the first.

He is careful to keep the worrying explanation on the list. The point is not to dismiss it but to stop it from being the only one he can see.

Holding these side by side, he notices that most of them call for the same first step, which is to give back some of the space he has taken, whatever else turns out to be going on.

steps.label: Ask about the space
steps.text:
Tom does not ask whether she regrets the move, which would put the whole relationship on trial. He says that he has realised he has been spreading out everywhere and taking her reading chair, and asks what would help the flat feel like hers as well as theirs. The question names the territory, not a feeling, and lets her say more if she wants to.

Starting with what he has noticed in himself, rather than what he has noticed in her, also makes the conversation easier for her to join.

steps.label: What happened
steps.text:
Leah laughs, a little embarrassed, and says that yes, she has been feeling like a guest in her own home. They agree that the armchair and the bookshelf stay hers, that Tom will turn the spare room into somewhere he can work and leave his things, and that they will buy one new piece of furniture together that is theirs from the start. The shortness stops within a week. Tom notes for himself that the most important things about moving in had not been said, and that the furniture had been saying them instead.

He also notes that the most useful reading in the whole episode was not of Leah's body at all, but of the flat.

moreFailures.title: Using home ground to win
moreFailures.body:
Once you know that people on their own territory tend to feel more confident and negotiate better, it is tempting to use it: always insisting on your office, keeping visitors waiting, choosing the seat with the window behind you, conducting disciplinary meetings on your own turf. In a negotiation between equals, some of this is ordinary hosting. But where the meeting is meant to be fair, such as a grievance, a difficult conversation with a junior, a dispute between neighbours or a family mediation, using territory to unsettle the other person is a way of winning on something other than the merits. Choose neutral ground when fairness matters, and if you must host, host generously: a good seat for the visitor, no waiting, water on the table.

It is worth noticing the reverse too: if you are always the visitor, in your manager's office, at your partner's family home, on your client's premises, some of your discomfort may be the ground rather than the people.

There is nothing wrong with feeling more at ease in your own office. The failure is arranging someone else's discomfort in order to profit from it.

moreFailures.title: Reading rooms as verdicts
moreFailures.body:
Gosling's work shows that rooms carry real information about their occupants, but it is partial, and it is easy to overreach. A cluttered home office says something about how its owner works; it does not say that he is incompetent. Expensive furniture and many books may reflect wealth and upbringing more than curiosity, and a bare room may reflect a recent move, a small budget or a tidy temperament rather than a lack of depth. On video calls, backgrounds are often chosen for the call, or blurred, or borrowed. Notice what rooms show, by all means, but treat it as a hint about habits and tastes, not a judgment of character, and never let it decide anything important, such as a hiring decision.

Interviewers who judge candidates by their video backgrounds are particularly at risk of judging class and circumstance rather than ability.

A reader who wants to learn from rooms might ask, instead, what the person has chosen to put where visitors will see it. That tells you what they want you to know about them, which is a different and more respectful thing to learn.

moreFailures.title: Overriding territory "for their own good"
moreFailures.body:
Families often rearrange an older parent's home for safety: moving the armchair, removing rugs, tidying away clutter, installing new furniture. Parents do the same with children's rooms, and carers with residents' rooms in care homes. The changes may be sensible, but when they are made without the person, they take away one of the last areas where that person is in charge, and the loss can show as anger, confusion or withdrawal that is then blamed on age or illness. Ask first, explain the reason, change one thing at a time, and leave the person's most important places, the chair, the bedside, the photographs, exactly where they are unless there is a real danger.

In care homes, residents' rooms are often the only primary territory they have left. Staff who knock, ask and leave things where they are give back a measure of control that matters far more than it seems.

A useful question for any change to someone else's space is whether you would accept the same change in your own home without being asked. If not, ask them.

moreFailures.title: Fighting a marker war
moreFailures.body:
Territorial disputes escalate through markers: a towel on a sunbed answered with a towel on the next one, a note on a windscreen answered with a bin in a parking space, a bag on a seat answered with a coat on the next seat. Each move feels justified, and each invites a stronger reply. The dispute is usually fought entirely through objects, without either party ever speaking to the other. If you notice yourself in one, ask whether the space is worth the conflict, and whether a single conversation might end it. Most of the time it would, because what each side wants is to be acknowledged, and an object cannot do that.

Holiday sunbeds are the comic version. The serious version happens between neighbours, siblings and former partners, where the objects stand in for grievances nobody has said aloud.

The same pattern runs through divorces and family inheritances, where the house, the furniture and the family photographs become the ground on which much older disputes are fought.

questions.q: Why do people get so upset about seats, desks and parking spaces?
questions.a:
Because these places are bound up with identity and belonging, not just convenience. A regular seat says that you are part of the place. A personalised desk says who you are at work. A parking space outside your house says that the street knows you. When someone takes one of these, it can feel like being told that you do not belong, or that you count for less than you thought. That is why territorial disputes so often feel out of proportion. Research on drivers by Ruback and Juieng even found people slower to leave a car park space when someone was waiting for it, as if defending a claim they were about to give up. The feelings are real, even when the claims have no legal standing.

If you are the one who has lost a space, it can help to name what it meant: not just a seat but a place where you belonged. Saying that, even to yourself, often takes some of the heat out of the anger.

Knowing this does not make every claim legitimate, but it makes it easier to respond to the feeling rather than the object, which is usually what ends the dispute.

A little acknowledgement goes a long way.

It is a trade-off, and Elsbach's research suggests it costs more than many organisations expect. Without a fixed desk, people lose a way of showing who they are and where they belong, and some feel it as a threat to their identity at work. Others prefer the flexibility, especially if they work from home often. Organisations that soften the change tend to do better: team zones rather than a free-for-all, lockers where people can keep personal things, permission to personalise a desk for the day, and attention to people who seem to have lost the most, such as long-serving staff who had built their place over years.

If you manage people through such a change, watch for those who seem to have lost the most, and give them something back, even something small, such as first choice of a desk in the new layout.

If you work in a hot-desking office yourself, small rituals help: a mug you always use, a plant you carry to whichever desk you take, a photograph on your laptop's lock screen.

questions.q: How should I behave in someone else's home?
questions.a:
As a guest on primary territory, which means letting the host lead. Wait to be offered a seat, or ask where to sit, because many homes have chairs that belong to particular people. Do not move things, open cupboards or go into rooms you have not been invited into. Follow the host's customs on shoes, food and where to put your coat. Notice the markers: a chair with a cushion and a reading lamp, a side of the sofa with the remote control, a seat at the table nobody else takes. These small courtesies cost nothing and tell the host that you understand you are on their ground.

If you are staying for longer, as a houseguest or a new partner, ask the host to show you where you can put your things. It saves you from guessing, and it shows that you know whose home it is.

If you are staying the night, the same rules apply more strongly to bedrooms and bathrooms, which are among the most private spaces in any home.

And when you leave, put things back as you found them: the chair you moved, the cushion you sat on, the cup you used. Hosts notice, and they remember guests who left their home as they found it.

questions.q: What do video call backgrounds tell me?
questions.a:
Less than they seem to. A background is a curated piece of territory: people choose what to show, tidy what is visible and often move to a better-looking room for calls. Many use blurred or virtual backgrounds precisely to avoid being read. What you can sometimes see is the setting of someone's working life, such as a child's drawing on the wall, a bed in the corner because there is no other room, or a busy kitchen, and that can tell you something about the pressures they are under. Treat it with discretion. Commenting on someone's home on a call, even kindly, can feel intrusive.

Your own background is also a choice. If you would rather not be read, a plain wall or a blurred background is perfectly acceptable.

questions.q: How can two people share a home without fighting over space?
questions.a:
By talking about territory before it becomes a fight. Each person usually needs at least one place that is clearly theirs: a desk, a chair, a shelf, a corner of a room, a drawer. Shared spaces work better when the rules are spoken rather than assumed: where things go, who uses which room when, how much of a shared surface each person may fill. When one person moves into a home that was the other's, it helps to change something together, so that the space starts to be shared rather than lent. And when a dispute about a small thing feels big, ask what the space means rather than arguing about the space.

Couples who have lived together for decades often say that the best decision they made was agreeing early on that each of them had one room, or one corner, that was theirs to arrange however they liked.

It also helps to agree how you will raise space problems before they arise, so that a complaint about a shelf can be made as a request rather than a rebuke.

questions.q: Is it rude to save seats with a coat or bag?
questions.a:
It depends on the setting and the norms. In a café, leaving a coat on a chair while you queue is widely accepted. In a crowded train or a busy library, saving seats for absent friends while others stand is often resented, and Sommer and Becker's work shows that markers can hold space long after the claim is reasonable. A good rule is to hold only what you will use soon, and to give way gracefully when the space is needed by someone who is actually there, especially someone older, pregnant or less able to stand.

On commuter trains, a bag on the seat beside you during the rush hour is one of the commonest small irritations people report, and one of the easiest to fix.

If you notice that someone has saved a seat that is now needed, a polite question to the people nearby usually resolves it faster than moving the marker yourself.

watch.title: Don't Mess With Sheldon's Spot!
watch.notice: A comic compilation built on one man's claim to a single seat on a sofa. Exaggerated, but recognisable: notice how the others work around claimed territory, and what happens when it is taken.

reviewPrompt: This week, ask before using one space that is usually someone else's, and notice how they respond.
